stem: A client receiving prenatal care from a certified nurse-midwife (CNM) asks what care a CNM may provide. Which response by the RN is most accurate?

options.A: CNM care is limited to prenatal visits and childbirth, with postpartum and primary care transferred to other clinicians.
options.B: CNMs may provide prenatal, childbirth, postpartum, gynecologic, family-planning, primary, and newborn care, subject to jurisdiction requirements.
options.C: CNMs practice only in hospitals and birth centers, so office, public-health, and home settings are outside the role.
options.D: CNMs have identical legal authority in every state because national certification creates a uniform scope of practice.

rationale: B is correct. NCSBN's current APRN Consensus Model Toolkit describes the CNM role as providing a full range of primary health care services throughout the lifespan, including gynecologic care, family planning, preconception care, prenatal and postpartum care, childbirth, and newborn care, in diverse settings. NCSBN also states that APRN regulatory requirements continue to differ by jurisdiction. A is incorrect because the nationally described CNM role extends beyond prenatal care and childbirth. C is incorrect because NCSBN explicitly includes settings such as homes, hospitals, birth centers, private offices, and community/public-health clinics. D is incorrect because national certification does not create identical legal authority across states; APRNs must meet the regulatory requirements of the jurisdiction in which the patient is located.
educational_objective: Recognize the broad nationally described CNM role across reproductive, primary, childbirth, postpartum, and newborn care while confirming that actual legal authority and practice requirements remain jurisdiction-specific.
source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: APRN Consensus Model Toolkit; APRN Consensus Model
source_version_date: Current NCSBN web resources accessed 2026-08-17; Consensus Model framework originally released 2008 with current NCSBN implementation guidance
source_locator: APRN Consensus Model Toolkit — Scope of Practice — Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM): full range of primary health care services, including gynecologic care, family planning, preconception care, prenatal and postpartum care, childbirth, and newborn care, delivered in diverse settings including home, hospital, birth center, offices, and community/public-health clinics. APRN Consensus Model — Moving Toward Uniformity: states have not adopted all Consensus Model elements, regulatory requirements differ from state to state, and APRNs must meet requirements where the patient is located.
source_claim_supported: The nationally described CNM role spans primary and reproductive health care, pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum and newborn care in diverse settings, while actual APRN regulatory authority remains jurisdiction-specific.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care, page 7; Related Activity Statements from the 2024 RN Practice Analysis include 'Identify and collaborate with multidisciplinary team members when providing client care' and 'Assess the need for referrals and obtain necessary orders.'
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — understanding provider roles for coordination of maternal and primary care
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic scope-definition item around current NCSBN APRN regulatory guidance. The final item explicitly separates the nationally described CNM role from jurisdiction-specific legal authority, eliminating the source version's risk of implying a universally identical scope across states.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: APRN/CNM role and scope / care coordination / Management of Care
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against NCSBN's current APRN Consensus Model Toolkit and APRN Consensus Model implementation page. NCSBN directly describes CNM services and settings and separately warns that state regulatory requirements are not uniform.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: B reproduces the scope domains identified by NCSBN while adding the necessary jurisdiction qualifier. A omits postpartum and primary care. C contradicts NCSBN's list of diverse practice settings. D contradicts NCSBN's explicit statement that regulatory requirements differ among jurisdictions.
audit_findings.choice_A: Incorrect but plausible; CNM care is broader than pregnancy and childbirth alone.
audit_findings.choice_B: Correct; accurately summarizes the nationally described CNM role without converting that description into a universal state-law claim.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect but plausible; CNMs may practice in multiple ambulatory, community, home, hospital, and birth-center settings.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect but plausible regulatory misconception; certification does not eliminate jurisdiction-specific APRN requirements.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B simultaneously reflects the NCSBN role description and jurisdictional variability. Each alternative conflicts with an explicit NCSBN statement.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address either breadth, setting, or regulatory scope of the CNM role and are similar in length and specificity; no implausible administrative-only distractor remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: Understanding the role and limits of another licensed care professional supports appropriate collaboration, referrals, and coordination under Management of Care.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited the item with special attention to state-law variability. Removed any implication that the Consensus Model itself creates legal authority in every jurisdiction. Rechecked services, settings, role terminology, and NCLEX relevance. No unresolved scope conflict or second answer remained.
